title: Defending American Property Abroad Act of 2026
official_title: To amend title 46, United States Code, with respect to the types of vessels that may enter or operate in navigable waters of the United States or transfer cargo in any port or place under the jurisdiction of the United States, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Pfluger (R-TX) with a bipartisan group of cosponsors (including Reps. Carbajal and Sewell); passed the House. A targeted maritime measure aimed at protecting U.S.-owned port property has bipartisan support, though it has not yet received a Senate vote.
summary: Lets the President restrict ships from entering U.S. ports if they used a port in a Western Hemisphere free-trade partner country that seized port property owned by a U.S. company.
brief: Allows the President to bar from U.S. ports vessels that used a Western Hemisphere free-trade-partner port expropriated from a U.S. owner.

top_lines.headline: Port Entry Restrictions
subs: President may designate expropriated foreign ports
Vessels using designated ports restricted from U.S. ports

top_lines.headline: Removal of Designation
subs: Designation lifted once the country restores ownership (and terminates any seizure measures) or pays adequate compensation

items.main: Names the Act the “Defending American Property Abroad Act of 2026”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Condition for Entry into Ports in the United States

items.main: Lets the President designate foreign ports that expropriated U.S.-owned port property, restricting vessels that used them from entering U.S. ports.
items.detail: Amends Section 70022 of title 46. The President may designate a port, harbor, or marine terminal in a Western Hemisphere country with a U.S. free trade agreement if that country nationalized or expropriated port property owned or controlled by a U.S. person and the port is accessible only through U.S.-person-controlled land. Vessels that transited a designated port become subject to the title's port-entry restriction. The President must remove a designation if the country restores ownership of the property and terminates any measures that had the effect of seizing ownership or possession, adequate compensation is paid, the conditions no longer apply, or the dispute is otherwise resolved. Emergencies and owner-authorized transits are excepted.

criticisms.why: the question is: Do we support President Trump with this authority? Absolutely, we do. This legislation makes it clear: The United States will not stand for unlawful harassment campaigns against American companies and American workers. For over 35 years, Vulcan Materials Company, based in Alabama, has lawfully owned and operated a limestone quarry in Mexico. Yet, since 2018, the Mexican Government has unlawfully restricted Vulcan's operations and wrongfully targeted them through coercion and intimidation.

This legislation codifies the commonsense principle that foreign nations should not profit from properties stolen from Americans. This bill is needed because for years the Mexican Government has engaged in a deliberate campaign against an American company, Vulcan Materials, headquartered in my district. In 2022, Mexican authorities used military force to shut down Vulcan's lawful operations. Then, in 2024, they took the dramatic step of declaring Vulcan's private property a protected natural area.

gaps: The bill targets Western Hemisphere free-trade partners but does not address expropriated port property elsewhere in the world.
It excludes matters in pending free-trade-agreement arbitration but sets no deadline for resolving such disputes.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Pfluger
featured_quotes.text: Let's be clear, American companies operating abroad should not have to fear arbitrary government actions that undermine their property rights, but right now, that is exactly what is happening. When countries violate trade agreements and illegally seize assets from U.S. companies, it puts American job security, economic security, and, quite frankly, our national security at risk. H.R. 7084 ensures there are enforceable consequences for those actions. Specifically, it strengthens U.S. maritime security law to address these unlawful seizures.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Moore
featured_quotes.text: what we have seen happen to Alabama's own Vulcan Materials Company should concern every Member of this body. A foreign government shut down an American company's operations, moved to seize its property, and ignored the rule of law. If it can happen to one American company, it can happen to any of them. We must protect American jobs and American investments and stand on the principles that the United States will stand for its people and its companies wherever they operate.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Garcia
featured_quotes.text: I rise today to voice my strong opposition to this bill. First of all, this bill and the substance of the bill, this dispute, is undergoing consideration by the international bodies established by the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade agreement. We really should wait until a decision is arrived at with respect to that mechanism, but there are other considerations. First, let's consider other far-reaching implications.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Aderholt
featured_quotes.text: today, the U.S. House of Representatives is acting in response to a situation in which a foreign government shut down an American company's operations, seized its property, and ignored the rule of law. When an American business is targeted in this way, it is not just an attack on one company, it is an attack on American workers, American jobs, and American interests. Vulcan Materials, an Alabama company, has lawfully operated for 35 years in Mexico. Yet the Mexican government illegally seized its assets.
